text: The advantages of being bilingual
A

I am sitting in a laboratory looking at snowflakes on a computer. As the snowflakes appear, I must decide which snowflake I hear being described in an invented language called Syntaflake. It's part of an experiment by Panos Athanasopoulos, Professor of Psycholinguistics at Lancaster University in England. The task feels impossible. Usually, when interacting in a language            that is less familiar to you, clues help decipher meaning. Speakers might point  to something, use their hands to demonstrate shape or fingers for numbers.               Here I have no help. Eventually I feel some kind of system is emerging with the syntax and sounds and I try to note it down. Later, I discover my approach was wrong. Athanasopoulos says: 'It's impossible in the time given to decipher the rules of the language and make sense of what's being said to you. But your brain is primed to work it out subconsciously. That's why, if you don't think about it, you'll do okay in the test.'

text: B

This innate capacity for understanding is part of language evolution. To communicate with other groups for trade and travel, our early ancestors would have found it necessary to speak other tongues. We know culture and language are deeply connected, so what happens when we speak two? Athanasopoulos  has been studying the capacity for language to change people's perspectives. In an earlier experiment, English and German speakers were shown videos of people moving, like a woman walking towards her car or a man cycling to the supermarket. English speakers focus on the action and describe the scene as 'a woman is walking' or 'a man is cycling'. German speakers have a more holistic world view, and include the goal of the action, saying 'a woman walks towards her car' or 'a man cycles towards the supermarket'.

text: C

This is partly due to grammar. Unlike German, English has the -ing ending to describe ongoing actions. This makes English speakers less likely to assign a  goal to an action when describing ambiguous scenes. When Athanasopoulos tested English-German bilinguals, however, whether they were action or goal-focused depended on where they were tested. If tested in Germany, they were goal-focused; in Britain, they were action-focused, no matter which language  was used, showing how intertwined culture and language can be in           determining our world view. In the 1960s, Susan Ervin-Tripp tested Japanese-English bilingual women, asking them to finish sentences in each language. 'When my wishes conflict with my family...' was completed in Japanese as 'it is         a time of great unhappiness'; in English, as 'I do what I want'. Ervin-Tripp concluded human thought takes place within language mindsets, and that bilinguals have different mindsets for each language.

text: D

But do bilinguals really have two separate minds? That's what the snowflake experiment was designed to discover. Volunteers like myself take 'flanker tests'         – which require you to ignore your instinctive responses – before and after the Syntaflake task. During the flanker tests, you click either the left or right keyboard arrow, to match the central arrow in a confusing pattern of other arrows on your screen. Most people do better after doing the Syntaflake task.  The brain area involved is the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC). It enables us to concentrate on one task while blocking out competing information. The snowflake test prepared my ACC for that second flanker test, just as speaking two languages trains it regularly. Bilinguals exercise their ACC constantly because their two languages compete for attention. But as cognitive neurologist Thomas Bak points out, bilinguals rarely mix them up, although they may introduce phrases from the other language if the listener also knows it.

text: E

Studies have shown that bilinguals outperform monolinguals in many cognitive and social tasks, including how well they can read other people. Greater  empathy is possible because bilinguals are better at blocking out their own beliefs and emotions in order to concentrate on someone else's. Another           exciting benefit of bilingualism occurs in ageing. When psycholinguist Ellen Bialystok of York University compared an elderly population of monolinguals  and bilinguals at risk of getting dementia – the inability to recall information – she found that the effects were significantly delayed in the latter group.

text: F

There has been a backlash against the studies showing bilingualism's benefits, as some researchers tried and failed to replicate certain results, leaving them unconvinced. But Bak says there is overwhelming evidence that bilingual         brains function differently. Bialystok admits we can't know whether           bilingualism improves exam scores because there are many confounding          factors. But, she says, 'given that no study has ever shown it harms performance, considering the very many social and cultural benefits to         knowing another language, bilingualism should be encouraged'.

text: G

One way to do this is through immersion schooling, in which children are         taught in another language half the time. Schools in Utah, USA, now offer immersion in Spanish or Chinese. 'We use a half-day model, so the target language is used to teach in the morning, and then English is used in the afternoon,' explains language specialist Gregg Roberts. This schedule is         regularly changed around, as levels of concentration among individual          students vary according to the time of day. Roberts reports that bilingual students do generally better than monolingual counterparts in every area of the curriculum, and have far more confidence in themselves. At Bohunt school in Hampshire, UK, head teacher Neil Strowger has introduced Chinese-language immersion for certain lessons, including art. Strowger says the programme has lifted not only students' grades and level of engagement, but increased their awareness of a culture other than their own. Another benefit is that the ability         to communicate in another language should be advantageous when it comes to seeking a rewarding career, something their parents are pleased to hear.
